title: Can you structure these 8 pricing and product launch case questions in two minutes each?
description: 8 pricing and product launch case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Yes, with two habits. For pricing, build a range from three sides (the cost floor, the customer's value ceiling and competitors' prices) and then test the volume you need. For launches, choose the target customer before anything else, because the product, price, channel and marketing all follow from that choice. Here are eight prompts: two minutes each, then open the model.
body:
How to use this set

Give yourself two minutes per prompt. For pricing prompts, your buckets will usually be cost, customer value, competitors and price structure, as in the three ways to set a price. For launch prompts, start with who the customer is, then what you sell them, where and how, and whether it pays, as in how to plan a product launch. Watch every prompt for cannibalisation: it is the most common hidden cost in this set.

1. What price should a company charge for fast EV charging?

Show a model structure
  • Cost floor: electricity, grid fees and equipment per kWh; the utilisation needed to break even.
  • Customer value: cost of charging at home versus on the road; time saved and convenience.
  • Competitors: rivals' prices and subscriptions; fuel cost per mile as a reference point.
  • Structure: per kWh, per minute or subscription; peak and off-peak prices.

Where to start: cost floor against value ceiling. The price sits between the two, and competitors show where in that range customers will accept it.

The trap: copying rivals' prices without knowing your own cost and utilisation.

2. How should a snack brand launch a high-protein bar?

Show a model structure
  • Who: target customers and their need; size of the segment.
  • What: product, flavours and pack sizes; price against rivals.
  • Where and how: supermarkets, gyms or online; marketing and sampling.
  • Economics and risks: volume to break even; cannibalisation of our other bars.

Where to start: who. A launch without a clear target customer spreads money thin.

The trap: starting with advertising before choosing the customer and the channel.

3. Should a supermarket launch a premium own-label range?

Show a model structure
  • Customer demand: shoppers buying premium brands; willingness to trust our brand at a higher price.
  • Economics: margin against branded products; volume needed to cover development.
  • Suppliers: who can make it at the right quality; how the big brands react.
  • Cannibalisation: sales taken from our standard own-label; net margin gained.

Where to start: margin against branded products. Own-label usually earns the retailer more per item.

The trap: ignoring how big brands might respond, for example by pulling promotional funding.

4. Should a business school launch a fully online MBA?

Show a model structure
  • Demand: students who cannot study on campus; the price they would pay.
  • Competition: other online MBAs and their prices; our brand against theirs.
  • Economics: development and teaching cost; students needed to break even.
  • Cannibalisation and brand: students switching from the campus MBA; perceived quality and rankings.

Where to start: cannibalisation of the campus MBA, often the school's flagship programme.

The trap: assuming every online student is new.

5. Should an electronics retailer introduce a price-match guarantee?

Show a model structure
  • Customer impact: extra sales from shoppers' confidence; share of customers who would claim.
  • Cost: margin given up on matched sales; admin to check claims.
  • Competitor response: rivals matching back and a price war; online-only rivals.
  • Rules: which rivals and products qualify; in store versus online.

Where to start: cost. If 5% of $1B of sales were matched at an average 8% discount, the guarantee would cost $4M a year, so the extra sales must earn more than that.

The trap: assuming only a few customers will claim.

6. Should a design-software company add a free plan?

Show a model structure
  • Acquisition: new users attracted; conversion from free to paid.
  • Cannibalisation: paying users moving down; what the free plan leaves out.
  • Costs: hosting and support for free users; fraud and abuse.
  • Competition: rivals' free plans; how customers choose a tool.

Where to start: conversion from free to paid against paying users who downgrade.

The trap: counting sign-ups as success.

7. Should a streaming service launch a cheaper plan with ads?

Show a model structure
  • New subscribers: people who find the full price too high; former subscribers won back.
  • Downgrades: current subscribers switching down; revenue lost per switch.
  • Ad revenue: ads per hour and the price advertisers pay; viewer experience.
  • Capability: ad sales team and technology; content rights that allow ads.

Where to start: downgrades. If the full plan is $15 a month and the ad plan $8, ads must earn at least $7 a month from each downgrader just to break even on them.

The trap: counting only the new subscribers.

8. How should an insurer launch weather insurance for small farmers in Kenya?

Show a model structure
  • Farmers' need: losses from drought and floods; what they can afford.
  • Product design: payouts triggered by rainfall data; price and cover.
  • Distribution: mobile money, co-operatives and seed sellers; bundling with loans.
  • Economics and risk: claims in a bad year hitting many farmers at once; reinsurance and government support.

Where to start: distribution. Reaching small farmers cheaply decides whether the product can work at all.

The trap: designing a product farmers cannot afford or reach.

How to score your answer: turn a price into a volume test

Take the charging prompt. Suppose a station sells 1M kWh a year at $0.60 per kWh, with variable cost of $0.30. Contribution is 1M × $0.30 = $300k a year before fixed costs. Raise the price to $0.70 and contribution per kWh rises to $0.40. To keep $300k, the station now needs only $300k ÷ $0.40 = 750,000 kWh. So the price rise pays as long as volume falls by less than 25%.

Strong: "A 17% price rise is worth it unless we lose more than a quarter of our volume. The question is whether drivers here have a convenient alternative."

That threshold tells you what to research: are there rival chargers nearby, is the site uniquely convenient, and would idle chargers raise the fixed cost per kWh? For launches, use the same discipline: a sized target customer, expected take-up, contribution per unit and the evidence you would need before scaling up. See price elasticity explained for the theory behind the test.
